n: Jerusalem had walls but few residents (Nehemiah 7:4). Leaders already lived there, and the people drew lots so that one family in ten would move into the city. Jerusalem is called “the holy city” because the temple was there.

f.g: A way of letting God decide (Proverbs 16:33).

n: Some also volunteered, and the people blessed them. Moving to Jerusalem meant leaving farms and family land for a more dangerous, less comfortable life.
This introduces the list of leaders living in Jerusalem. Everyone else lived on their own family property in the towns of Judah.

f.g: On his inherited family land.

n: Residents from the tribe of Judah are listed first. Athaiah’s line traces to Perez, the son of Judah through whom King David descended — and, Matthew notes, Jesus.
Another Judahite family head, descended from Shelah (here “Shiloni”), another son of Judah.

f.g: A Shelanite — descendant of Shelah son of Judah (Numbers 26:20).

n: The Perez clan in Jerusalem numbered 468 capable men.

f.g: Able, strong men — capable of defending the city.

n: Now the residents from Benjamin, the small tribe whose territory bordered Jerusalem.
Benjamin’s men in Jerusalem numbered 928 — twice as many as Judah’s, perhaps because Jerusalem lay on Benjamin’s border.

f.g: A large number relative to Judah’s 468.

n: Two officials governed the city’s residents: Joel as overseer and Judah son of Senuah as second in command, perhaps over a newer district.

f.g: Deputy, or possibly in charge of the “Second Quarter” of the city (compare Zephaniah 1:10).

n: The priests living in Jerusalem are named next.
Seraiah, of the high priestly line of Zadok, was in charge of the temple.

f.w: the ruler of the house of God
f.g: The chief officer of the temple, under the high priest.

n: Over 800 priests did the work of the temple. Adaiah’s family traced back to Pashur and Malchiah.

f.w: did the work of the house
f.g: Served in the temple’s daily rites.

n: Heads of priestly families numbered 242, including Amashai of the house of Immer.

f.g: Heads of family households.

n: Another 128 strong, capable priests served under an overseer named Zabdiel.

f.w: the son of one of the great men
f.g: Possibly a proper name, “son of Haggedolim.”

n: Levites in the holy city are listed next.
Two senior Levites managed the temple’s outside affairs — perhaps collecting supplies and tithes and maintaining the buildings.

f.g: Practical work outside the temple’s sacred rituals.

n: Mattaniah, a descendant of David’s musician Asaph, led the thanksgiving prayers — the temple choir director. Jeduthun was another of David’s chief musicians.

f.w: to begin the thanksgiving in prayer
f.g: To lead the singing of thanksgiving psalms.

n: There were 284 Levites in Jerusalem — still far fewer than the priests.

f.g: 284 (fourscore = 80).

n: The gatekeepers, who guarded the temple and city gates, numbered 172.

f.g: Gatekeepers.

n: Everyone else lived on their inherited land in Judah’s towns.

f.g: The rest, remainder.

n: The temple servants lived on Ophel, the hill just south of the temple, close to their work.
Uzzi, also a descendant of Asaph, supervised the Levites. The singers had charge over the music in the house of God.

f.w: the singers were over the business of the house of God

n: By order of the Persian king, the singers received a daily allowance. Royal support helped the temple music continue.

f.g: A fixed allowance or ration.

n: Pethahiah, of Judah’s clan of Zerah, served as the people’s representative to the king — an adviser or agent for Jewish affairs at court.

f.g: The king’s agent or adviser in matters concerning the Jews.

n: Now the towns and villages of Judah. Kirjath-arba is the old name for Hebron, where Abraham was buried.

f.g: The old name of Hebron (Joshua 14:15).
A town in southern Judah, not the Moabite Dibon.

n: More southern towns, in the region near the Negev desert.
Beer-sheba marked Israel’s traditional southern boundary and was associated with Abraham and Isaac.
Ziklag was the town David received from the Philistines while hiding from Saul.
Zareah (Zorah) was the hometown of Samson’s family.

f.g: Zorah, Samson’s hometown (Judges 13:2).

n: Adullam was where David hid in a cave; Lachish and Azekah were fortress towns. Judah’s people now stretched from Beer-sheba in the south to the Hinnom Valley at Jerusalem.

f.g: The valley along Jerusalem’s south side.

n: The towns of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem, including Bethel where Jacob saw the heavenly ladder.
Anathoth was Jeremiah’s hometown; Nob was the priests’ town where David once received holy bread.
Ramah, a hometown of the prophet Samuel, is among these Benjamite towns.
Three smaller towns of Benjamin.

f.g: A Benjamite town, different from the city destroyed with Sodom (Genesis 14:2).

n: Lod and Ono lay in a valley known for its craftsmen.
Some groups of Levites lived in Judah and some in Benjamin, serving among the people wherever they lived.

f.g: Groups or courses of Levites.
